title: Two Annas a Ride: Dharampal Gulati's Tonga Before the Spice Shop
dek: Arriving in Delhi after Partition with Rs 1,500, Dharampal Gulati spent 650 on a horse cart before going back to his family's spice trade.

story.event: Driving a tonga in Delhi after Partition, then reopening the family spice business in a Karol Bagh shack
story.summary: Dharampal Gulati, whose family had left its Sialkot spice shop in the Partition riots, reached Delhi on 27 September 1947 with Rs 1,500 and spent Rs 650 on a tonga, carrying passengers for two annas a ride. Finding the work draining and poorly paid, he gave it up and reopened the family trade in a small wooden shop in Karol Bagh, advertising it in the Hindi paper Pratap as Mahashian di Hatti of Sialkot; the business grew into the MDH spice company.
paragraphs: On 27 September 1947, Dharampal Gulati reached Delhi by train with two relatives and Rs 1,500. He was 24 and had left school before finishing Class 5. Until the Partition riots he had worked in his father's spice shop in Sialkot, Mahashian di Hatti, known locally for its deggi mirch. The family had left the shop, their house and their cattle behind. In Delhi they crowded into an abandoned house his sister had claimed in Karol Bagh, with little room to sleep, no running water and no latrine, and registered for refugee ration cards.

He did not go straight back to spices. In Chandni Chowk, where tongas were being sold, he bargained for a horse cart and paid 650 rupees, close to half his money. "I used to wait near the railway station and say 'two annas sawari, two annas'," he later told the writer Mallika Ahluwalia. He carried passengers between New Delhi station, Qutab Road, Karol Bagh and Bara Hindu Rao. By her account he found the other drivers rough and the work draining, for little money. He gave it up, and a small stall selling cane sugar went no better.

What he settled on was the trade the family knew best. He opened a small wooden roadside shop, by the company's own account a khokha of 14 feet by 9 on Ajmal Khan Road in Karol Bagh, selling ground spices under the old name. To find customers he placed an advertisement in the Hindi newspaper Pratap: "Mahashian di Hatti of Sialkot Deggi Mirch Waale". Orders came by post, Ahluwalia writes, one of the first from a businessman in Cuttack who had himself come from Multan.

He ended a partnership with a man who mixed lentils into the spices to sell them cheaper. He opened another shop in Khari Baoli, Delhi's main spice market, and from 1949 sold spices in designed boxes. In 1959 he bought land in Kirti Nagar, and by the 1960s he had a factory. MDH became one of India's best-known spice brands, and in old age Gulati, in a red turban, appeared in its television advertisements himself.

quote.text: We see in needle-works and embroideries, it is more pleasing to have a lively work, upon a sad and solemn ground, than to have a dark and melancholy work, upon a lightsome ground
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon does not call hardship good. He notices that bright work set on a dark ground moves us more than the reverse. Gulati's first advertisement kept the lost city in the shop's name, 'of Sialkot', as if the ground were part of the pattern.

reflection: The tonga is easy to skip in this story, but it may be the most honest part. Gulati had lost a shop, a house and a city, and the first thing he tried was not his family's trade but whatever he could buy that week. It did not suit him, and he stopped.

You may have a detour like that of your own: a job or a plan chosen because something had to be done. It need not be counted as wasted. Sometimes it is how you learn which work you actually know how to do.
invitation: Think of one thing you tried that did not suit you. Write down one thing it taught you about the work you do know how to do, and leave it at that.

cross_checks.claim: Gulati reached Delhi on 27 September 1947 with Rs 1,500.
He spent Rs 650 on a tonga and carried passengers for two annas a ride.
He then restarted the family spice trade in a small wooden shop on Ajmal Khan Road, Karol Bagh.
He advertised in the Hindi newspaper Pratap as 'Mahashian di Hatti of Sialkot Deggi Mirch Waale'.
The business moved to its own land in Kirti Nagar in 1959 and had a factory by the 1960s.

research_notes: How long he drove the tonga is unclear: Business Today and The Weekend Leader, both drawing on MDH's own bio-sketch, say 'for a few days', while the PTI report in The Tribune, citing the same bio-sketch, says he sold the carriage in October 1948. The story gives no duration. The order of his early attempts also varies: the Ahluwalia material (via PTI and The Hitavada) mentions sugarcane selling and a cane-sugar stall around the tonga period; the story says only that the stall 'went no better'. The first shop is a 14 ft by 9 ft wooden khokha on Ajmal Khan Road in the company's account (Business Today, Weekend Leader, Tribune) and a 'small wooden roadside shop' in Ahluwalia's; one search snippet placed a 1948 plot on Khajoor Road, unconfirmed by any source read, so it is not used. Gulati's quotation is from Mallika Ahluwalia's interview-based book as excerpted in the PTI report on The News Minute; the book itself was not available online. The Weekend Leader also mentions a refugee camp in Amritsar, which the story omits since the PTI account says only that the family reached Amritsar first. His age at death is variously given as 97 and 98; it is not used. MDH's own website did not load. The Bacon passage is applied by analogy; it was written about adversity in general.
